title: “My Parents Were Teachers”: Blake Griffin Rips Thunder’s $850 Million Taxpayer-Funded Arena Deal
text:
“My Parents Were Teachers”: Blake Griffin Rips Thunder’s $850 Million Taxpayer-Funded Arena Deal - BasketballNews NBA Play Hoops Rank NBA Play Hoops Rank Home / News “My Parents Were Teachers”: Blake Griffin Rips Thunder’s $850 Million Taxpayer-Funded Arena Deal
 By
 Deblina Roy Nov 17, 2026, 3:24 AM CUT
 Imago
 IMAGO / Image Press Agency
 While the Oklahoma City Thunder are busy figuring out a winning trajectory amid injury heartbreaks this season, the city is ready to build the team a $900M arena by the 2029-30 NBA campaign. However, former NBA star Blake Griffin clearly believes the city could do better with all that money than what they’re set to do.
 “I grew up in Oklahoma City, born and raised, and when we got the Thunder it was super exciting, and fans are obviously crazy about them,” he said during an episode of The Stepback with Blake Griffin show. “It's a great team with a recent championship and a ton of pride. So much pride that the people of Oklahoma voted to pretty much buy the organization a new arena, spending 850 million dollars of taxpayer money while the owners are chipping in 50 million … those taxpayer dollars could go to a lot of things. Oklahoma ranks 45th in starting teacher pay, which matters to me because both my parents were teachers.”
 In detail, the city voted yes to build the $900M arena in an “overwhelming 71% to 29% split” in 2023. As taxpayers are set to pay a six-year penny sales tax that will cover the $850M, the ownership will take care of just about 5.5% of the expected cost. As per a 2023 Sports Business Journal report , “the Thunder have committed to playing in the new arena for 25 years, which would secure Oklahoma City's status as an NBA city through at least 2054.”
 Moreover, Oklahoma’s Mayor David Holt stated that the city didn’t really have any leverage in this negotiation. As per an April 1, 2026 report by the Oklahoma Gazette, “Forbes currently values the Thunder at $4.35 billion, a 1,143 per cent increase over two decades. According to Forbes, the team’s net operating income for the 2024-25 championship season was estimated at $114 million, following $74 million during the 2023-24 campaign.”
 Hence, not building a new facility would cost the city the team they love and cause the solid financial footing to decline. As Holt put it, building a new facility is “one of the first orders of business.”
 “Cities like ours never have leverage in these situations,” he told Front Office Sports, per the aforementioned Oklahoma Gazette report. “We in Oklahoma City haven’t had the team long enough to forget what it was like before we had the team.”
 As Griffin put it, the city that can’t afford to increase the starting teacher’s pay now just feels “hamstrung, having to pay billions of dollars to keep the teams they love.” Surely, to many economists, this is just one of the worst taxpayer deals. But for the city with little to no choice in this matter of a subsidized stadium, it definitely goes beyond sport.
